name: Chapter 12: Respiration in Plants
description: Gas exchange in plants, glycolysis, fermentation, Krebs cycle, ETS, ATP balance sheet, amphibolic pathway, RQ

cards.term: What is respiration?
cards.definition: Breaking of C–C bonds of complex compounds by oxidation within cells, releasing considerable energy

cards.term: What are respiratory substrates?
cards.definition: Compounds oxidised during respiration; usually carbohydrates, but also proteins, fats and organic acids

cards.term: Most common respiratory substrate?
cards.definition: Glucose (carbohydrates)

cards.term: Why is energy released step by step, not all at once?
cards.definition: So that small packets can be trapped as ATP instead of being lost as heat; each step is enzyme-controlled

cards.term: Why is ATP called the energy currency of the cell?
cards.definition: Energy from respiration is stored in ATP, which is broken down whenever and wherever energy is needed

cards.term: Besides ATP, what else does respiration provide?
cards.definition: Carbon skeletons used as precursors for biosynthesis

cards.term: Where does respiration occur in eukaryotic cells?
cards.definition: In the cytoplasm (glycolysis) and mitochondria

cards.term: Why do non-green plant parts need food translocated to them?
cards.definition: Only chloroplast-containing (usually superficial) cells photosynthesise; all other cells must oxidise food for energy

cards.term: How do plants exchange gases without respiratory organs?
cards.definition: Through stomata and lenticels

cards.term: Three reasons plants manage without respiratory organs?
cards.definition: (1) Each part handles its own gas exchange. (2) Plants have low demands (respire slowly). (3) Gases diffuse only short distances: living cells are near the surface.

cards.term: How do cells deep in woody stems get air?
cards.definition: Living cells are in thin layers beneath the bark with lenticels; interior cells are dead (support only)

cards.term: What helps air reach cells inside leaves, stems and roots?
cards.definition: Loosely packed parenchyma forming an interconnected network of air spaces

cards.term: Why don't photosynthesising cells lack O₂?
cards.definition: O₂ is released within the cell itself

cards.term: Complete combustion of glucose?
cards.definition: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (mostly heat)

cards.term: Respiration vs combustion?
cards.definition: Combustion: one step, energy lost as heat. Respiration: many enzyme steps, energy trapped as ATP.

cards.term: What did the first cells on earth likely use for energy?
cards.definition: Anaerobic pathways: the early atmosphere lacked oxygen

cards.term: Facultative vs obligate anaerobes?
cards.definition: Facultative: can live with or without O₂. Obligate: require anaerobic conditions.

cards.term: What machinery do all living organisms retain?
cards.definition: Enzymes to partially oxidise glucose without O₂: glycolysis

cards.term: Meaning of "glycolysis"?
cards.definition: Greek glycos = sugar, lysis = splitting

cards.term: Who gave the scheme of glycolysis?
cards.definition: Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas: the EMP pathway

cards.term: Where does glycolysis occur?
cards.definition: In the cytoplasm, in all living organisms

cards.term: In which organisms is glycolysis the only process of respiration?
cards.definition: Anaerobic organisms

cards.term: End product of glycolysis?
cards.definition: Two molecules of pyruvic acid (partial oxidation of glucose)

cards.term: Source of glucose for glycolysis in plants?
cards.definition: Sucrose (end product of photosynthesis) or storage carbohydrates

cards.term: Which enzyme converts sucrose to glucose and fructose?
cards.definition: Invertase

cards.term: Which enzyme phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate?
cards.definition: Hexokinase

cards.term: Correction: NCERT says glucose and fructose are both phosphorylated "to glucose-6-phosphate". What is precise?
cards.definition: Hexokinase makes glucose-6-phosphate from glucose and fructose-6-phosphate from fructose; both then follow the same path.

cards.term: How many reactions in glycolysis?
cards.definition: A chain of ten enzyme-controlled reactions

cards.term: At which two steps is ATP used in glycolysis?
cards.definition: Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate; fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate

cards.term: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into?
cards.definition: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL)

cards.term: At which step is NADH + H⁺ formed in glycolysis?
cards.definition: PGAL → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA): PGAL is oxidised and takes up Pi

cards.term: At which steps is ATP made in glycolysis?
cards.definition: BPGA → 3-PGA and PEP → pyruvic acid

cards.term: ATP count in glycolysis per glucose?
cards.definition: Used: 2. Made: 4 (2 steps × 2 trioses). Net: 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH.

cards.text: Glycolysis: glucose → {{c1::glucose-6-phosphate}} → {{c2::fructose-6-phosphate}} → {{c3::fructose-1,6-bisphosphate}} → PGAL + DHAP → {{c4::1,3-BPGA}} → {{c5::3-PGA}} → 2-PGA → {{c6::PEP}} → pyruvic acid.

cards.term: Which step of glycolysis releases water?
cards.definition: 2-phosphoglycerate → PEP

cards.term: Figure 12.1 · Steps of glycolysis
Three fates of pyruvic acid?
cards.definition: Lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation, aerobic respiration

cards.term: What happens in alcoholic fermentation (yeast)?
cards.definition: Pyruvic acid → CO₂ + ethanol under anaerobic conditions

cards.term: Two enzymes of alcoholic fermentation?
cards.definition: Pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase

cards.term: Which enzyme reduces pyruvic acid to lactic acid?
cards.definition: Lactate dehydrogenase

cards.term: When do animal muscles make lactic acid?
cards.definition: During exercise, when O₂ is inadequate

cards.term: What is the reducing agent in fermentation?
cards.definition: NADH + H⁺, reoxidised to NAD⁺

cards.term: Why is regenerating NAD⁺ the real purpose of fermentation?
cards.definition: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ at the PGAL step; without O₂, turning pyruvate into lactate or ethanol is the only way to recycle NADH so glycolysis keeps making ATP

cards.term: How much of glucose's energy does fermentation release?
cards.definition: Less than 7%, and not all of it is trapped as ATP

cards.term: Net ATP from fermentation of one glucose?
cards.definition: 2 ATP (from glycolysis)

cards.term: Why is fermentation hazardous?
cards.definition: It produces acid or alcohol

cards.term: At what alcohol concentration do yeasts poison themselves?
cards.definition: About 13%

cards.term: How are drinks stronger than 13% alcohol made?
cards.definition: Distillation of the fermented liquid

cards.term: Where does fermentation occur?
cards.definition: In many prokaryotes, unicellular eukaryotes and germinating seeds

cards.term: Fermentation vs aerobic respiration?
cards.definition: Fermentation: partial breakdown, net 2 ATP, NADH oxidised slowly. Aerobic: complete to CO₂ + H₂O, many ATP, NADH oxidised vigorously.

cards.term: What is aerobic respiration?
cards.definition: Complete oxidation of organic substances in the presence of O₂, releasing CO₂, water and much energy

cards.term: Two crucial events of aerobic respiration, and where?
cards.definition: (1) Complete oxidation of pyruvate by removing H atoms, leaving 3 CO₂: matrix. (2) Passing electrons to O₂ with ATP synthesis: inner membrane.

cards.term: What happens to pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix?
cards.definition: Oxidative decarboxylation to acetyl CoA, by pyruvic dehydrogenase

cards.term: Link reaction equation?
cards.definition: Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺ (Mg²⁺, pyruvate dehydrogenase)

cards.term: Coenzymes needed by pyruvate dehydrogenase?
cards.definition: NAD⁺ and coenzyme A (and Mg²⁺)

cards.term: NADH from the link reaction per glucose?
cards.definition: 2

cards.term: Other names of the Krebs cycle?
cards.definition: Tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, citric acid cycle

cards.term: First step of the Krebs cycle?
cards.definition: Acetyl group + OAA + water → citric acid, by citrate synthase; CoA released

cards.term: After citrate, what happens?
cards.definition: Isomerised to isocitrate, then two decarboxylations → α-ketoglutaric acid → succinyl-CoA

cards.term: Where is GTP made in the Krebs cycle?
cards.definition: Succinyl-CoA → succinic acid: substrate-level phosphorylation

cards.term: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?
cards.definition: ATP (or GTP) made directly from a substrate in a reaction, not through the ETS

cards.term: What happens to the GTP?
cards.definition: GTP → GDP, coupled with ADP → ATP

cards.term: How many NADH and FADH₂ points in one turn of the Krebs cycle?
cards.definition: 3 NAD⁺ → NADH; 1 FAD → FADH₂

cards.term: What must be replenished for the Krebs cycle to continue?
cards.definition: Oxaloacetic acid, plus NAD⁺ and FAD regenerated from NADH and FADH₂

cards.term: Krebs cycle summary equation (per pyruvate)?
cards.definition: Pyruvic acid + 4NAD⁺ + FAD + 2H₂O + ADP + Pi → 3CO₂ + 4NADH + 4H⁺ + FADH₂ + ATP

cards.term: Totals up to the end of the Krebs cycle (per glucose)?
cards.definition: 8 NADH (from link + Krebs), 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP in TCA; plus glycolysis's 2 NADH and 2 ATP

cards.term: Carbon count through the cycle?
cards.definition: Acetyl CoA (2C) + OAA (4C) → citric acid (6C) → α-ketoglutaric (5C) → succinic, malic, OAA (4C)

cards.term: Note on "FAD⁺" in NCERT?
cards.definition: FAD carries no charge. It is written FAD → FADH₂ (NAD⁺ does carry a charge).

cards.term: Figure 12.3 · Citric acid cycle
Why are O₂ and big ATP yields still missing after the Krebs cycle?
cards.definition: The energy is held in NADH and FADH₂; it is released only when they are oxidised through the ETS, with O₂ as the final acceptor

cards.term: Where is the ETS located?
cards.definition: In the inner mitochondrial membrane

cards.term: Where do electrons from NADH go first?
cards.definition: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) → ubiquinone

cards.term: How does FADH₂ enter the ETS?
cards.definition: Via complex II to ubiquinone (it bypasses complex I)

cards.term: Reduced ubiquinone is called?
cards.definition: Ubiquinol

cards.term: What is cytochrome c?
cards.definition: A small protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane; a mobile carrier between complex III and IV

cards.term: What does complex IV contain?
cards.definition: Cytochromes a and a₃ and two copper centres

cards.term: Mobile carriers of the ETS?
cards.definition: Ubiquinone (in the membrane) and cytochrome c

cards.term: ATP per NADH and per FADH₂ (NCERT)?
cards.definition: NADH: 3 ATP. FADH₂: 2 ATP.

cards.term: Why does FADH₂ give fewer ATP than NADH?
cards.definition: It enters at complex II, skipping complex I, so fewer protons are pumped

cards.term: Role of O₂ in aerobic respiration?
cards.definition: Final hydrogen (electron) acceptor, forming water; it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen

cards.term: Why is it called oxidative phosphorylation?
cards.definition: The proton gradient is made with energy from oxidation-reduction (vs light energy in photophosphorylation)

cards.term: ATP synthase in mitochondria: F₁ vs F₀?
cards.definition: F₁: peripheral headpiece with the ATP-making site. F₀: integral membrane channel for protons.

cards.term: How many H⁺ pass through F₀ per ATP?
cards.definition: 4 H⁺, from intermembrane space to matrix

cards.term: Direction of proton flow through mitochondrial ATP synthase?
cards.definition: Intermembrane space → matrix

cards.term: Chloroplast vs mitochondrion: where do protons pile up?
cards.definition: Chloroplast: thylakoid lumen (CF₀–CF₁). Mitochondrion: intermembrane space (F₀–F₁).

cards.term: Why does cyanide kill?
cards.definition: It blocks cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), so electrons cannot reach O₂ and ATP production stops

cards.term: Four assumptions for the ATP balance sheet?
cards.definition: (1) Sequential orderly pathway. (2) Glycolytic NADH enters mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation. (3) No intermediates used for other compounds. (4) Only glucose is respired.

cards.term: Why are these assumptions unrealistic?
cards.definition: Pathways run simultaneously substrates enter and leave as needed ATP is used as needed enzyme rates are controlled

cards.term: Net ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration (NCERT)?
cards.definition: 38 ATP

cards.term: 38 ATP balance sheet
cards.definition: Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH (6) = 8; Link reaction: 2 NADH = 6; Krebs cycle: 2 ATP + 6 NADH (18) + 2 FADH₂ (4) = 24; Total: 38

cards.term: Update: is 38 ATP what cells really get?
cards.definition: Modern values are about 30–32 ATP (≈2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂; shuttling glycolytic NADH costs energy). For exams, use NCERT's 38.

cards.term: Significance of step-wise energy release?
cards.definition: Energy is released in small packets that can be trapped as ATP, and intermediates can be used for biosynthesis

cards.term: Favoured respiratory substrate?
cards.definition: Glucose: other carbohydrates are usually converted to glucose first

cards.term: Where do fatty acids enter respiration?
cards.definition: As acetyl CoA

cards.term: Where does glycerol enter respiration?
cards.definition: As PGAL (3-phosphoglyceraldehyde)

cards.term: How do proteins enter respiration?
cards.definition: Proteases → amino acids → deamination → enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs intermediates

cards.term: Why is the respiratory pathway called amphibolic?
cards.definition: It serves both catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (e.g. acetyl CoA withdrawn to make fatty acids)

cards.term: Catabolism vs anabolism?
cards.definition: Catabolism: breaking down. Anabolism: synthesis.

cards.term: Define respiratory quotient (RQ).
cards.definition: Volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed. Also called respiratory ratio.

cards.term: RQ depends on what?
cards.definition: The type of respiratory substrate

cards.term: RQ of carbohydrates?
cards.definition: 1 (6 CO₂ / 6 O₂)

cards.term: RQ of fats? Example?
cards.definition: Less than 1: tripalmitin 102 CO₂ / 145 O₂ ≈ 0.7

cards.term: Tripalmitin oxidation equation?
cards.definition: 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O + energy

cards.term: RQ of proteins?
cards.definition: About 0.9

cards.term: Why is fat RQ below 1? (intuition)
cards.definition: Fats contain little oxygen, so extra O₂ is needed to oxidise their many H atoms to water; more O₂ used than CO₂ given out

cards.term: Beyond NCERT: RQ of organic acids and anaerobic respiration?
cards.definition: Organic acids (e.g. malic acid): > 1. Anaerobic respiration: ∞ (CO₂ released, no O₂ used).

cards.term: Are pure fats or proteins used as respiratory substrates?
cards.definition: Never. Usually more than one substrate is used.

cards.term: Location of respiratory steps
cards.definition: Glycolysis: Cytoplasm; Fermentation: Cytoplasm; Pyruvate → acetyl CoA: Mitochondrial matrix; Krebs cycle: Mitochondrial matrix; ETS, oxidative phosphorylation: Inner mitochondrial membrane
